quote: “So,” I said incredulously, “if God exists or doesn’t exist, that has absolutely no effect on how it would be good for people to think or act? I think even a rabbi would look a little askance at that.”
content: Orthopraxy is the priority of practice over doctrine; the woman's claim was stronger, that whether God exists has absolutely no bearing on how it would be good for people to think or act, which no orthoprax tradition holds — the Reconstructionist position is that the practices are valuable, not that the truth of the theology is irrelevant to what one should do. That is what the essay is expressing incredulity at, and a rabbi would indeed press it, because the tradition's own arguments about why to keep the commandments are arguments. The Jerusalem Talmud line is about the order of priority, not about the irrelevance of the object.

quote: you get the same sort of placebo benefit that would actually come from a successful self-deception
content: Lim and Putnam are evidence for the essay. If the measured benefits of religion run through attendance and congregational friendship and not through belief, then the placebo the woman is trying to install is not the thing delivering the goods, and her project of believing in order to receive them is misconceived — which is the essay's conclusion, reached by the annotation's citation. The essay's promise to aim at the placebo benefits is aimed at her belief that the belief is what pays, and the sociology says it is not.
